Text 1
Art critic James Holloway argues that museums should display artworks with minimal text, letting viewers form their own responses. Long labels, he claims, turn looking into reading and tell visitors what to think.

Text 2
Museum educator Ruth Okafor found that visitors who read brief contextual labels spent more time looking at paintings, not less, and later described more details of the works. Information, she suggests, can direct attention toward the art rather than away from it.
stem: Based on the texts, how would Okafor (Text 2) most likely respond to Holloway's claim (Text 1)?
choices: By arguing that her findings suggest labels can increase, rather than reduce, attention to artworks
By agreeing that viewers should form their own responses to art without being given any outside information
By claiming that long labels are more effective than brief labels in museums
By arguing that visitors spend too much time reading labels in most museums
steps: Holloway: text pulls attention away from art.
Okafor: visitors with brief labels looked longer and noticed more, so information can direct attention to the art.
She disagrees with him; she studied brief, not long, labels; and her data show more looking, not too much reading.
key: Check the details of Text 2's evidence (brief labels, more looking) against each choice.
